item.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ced7vj2gv82o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge - Published Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show. The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx. On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards. Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July. At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor. Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants. In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence". The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades." It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity. The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings. Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident. However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity. Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected". But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim. "They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party. Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes". The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30". A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response". Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing. "The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information." Related topics - Published2 September - Published1 September

item.title: Google picks Finland for its largest single investment in Europe
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r6y4me2g6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Google picks Finland for its largest single investment in Europe - Published Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced. The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services. "This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday. "Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement. As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent". Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers. Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres. The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028. "The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added. "Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties." Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009. The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube. Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development". "Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google. "This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added. Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services. The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity. Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity. item.title: Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvznqypz0yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes - Published Oil prices rose to $100 (£74) a barrel on Wednesday, after the US and Iran attacked tankers in the Gulf region and Yemen's Houthis hit oil facilities in Saudi Arabia. Overnight, the US said it struck five Iranian tankers in retaliation for Iran's targeting of a warship, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they attacked eight tankers and two warships in response, as well as a US base in Jordan. The Guards also said they planned a new "prohibited zone" for shipping that extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz into the Arabian Sea. The Iran-backed Houthis reported dozens of Saudi strikes in Yemen, a day after drone and missile attacks caused fires at several oil facilities in Saudi Arabia. The escalating conflicts pushed the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, to its highest level since late July, when Iran and the US resumed hostilities after a one-month lull. A barrel was priced at $100.70, up 2.83% compared to Tuesday, on Wednesday afternoon. Before the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February, Brent crude had been priced at about $70 (£52) a barrel. But Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial shipping and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports resulted in the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz waterway in the Gulf, through which 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments usually pass. The Houthis have also been targeting Saudi energy infrastructure and tankers in the Red Sea since July, when a four-year ceasefire in Yemen began unravelling. The rising oil costs have sparked leaps in petrol prices around the world for motorists. The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said early on Wednesday that its latest strikes destroyed four Iranian oil tankers linked to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) in the Gulf of Oman - Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco - and a fifth tanker - Derya - near Kharg Island, in the northern Gulf, which hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil. US forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck, it added. Centcom said the attacks came after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles at a US warship in the region twice in two days. It added that the warship "successfully evaded" the missiles and that no American troops were harmed. The IRGC said its Aerospace Force launched missiles at US maintenance facilities, hangars and aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan overnight in retaliation for the US strikes. Jordan's armed forces said they intercepted 20 Iranian missiles and two others fell in unpopulated areas, with no casualties were reported. Later, the IRGC said its navy also attacked two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels. Centcom said the claim that the IRGC struck two of its warships was false. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received reports of several merchant vessels in the northern Gulf and the Gulf of Oman being "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region". It also reported that one vessel 24 nautical miles (45km) north-west of Port Rashid, in the United Arab Emirates, was seen "listing while at anchor, possibly indicating water ingress following an attack from an unknown projectile". Iraqi authorities said they extinguished a fire on a Panama-flagged tanker, New Andros, that was carrying two million barrels of fuel oil when it was hit by a drone in the Gulf. On Wednesday afternoon, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi told Iranian state TV that it would soon announce the co-ordinates for a new "prohibited zone" covering "part of the Sea of Oman and another part of the Arabian Sea, along the route that can lead to the Strait of Hormuz". "If a vessel enters that area without co-ordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," he said. When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the situation was "pretty straightforward". "Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip to Colombia. The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's Navy said it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz. US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said an "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and that it had been used to survey regional waters. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, an Iran-backed group that controls much of north-western Yemen, have also been exchanging fire. Following a wave of air strikes on Sunday and Monday, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in Hazm. The group's military spokesman Yahya Sarea said on Wednesday that the bodies of 23 civilians had so far been pulled from the rubble. On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at civilian and economic sites in the southern Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring 73 civilians, according to Saudi authorities. The attacks caused fires at oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, they said. On Wednesday, the Houthis reported more than 50 Saudi air strikes across territory they control in the provinces of Marib, Jawf, Taiz, Hudaydah, Saada and Bayda. There was no immediate comment from the Saudi military. There has also been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. More than 500 people have reportedly been killed and almost 20,000 displaced. - Published4 days ago - Published3 days ago

item.title: Iran referred to UN Security Council for nuclear non-compliance
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgwj4kl5lno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran referred to UN Security Council for nuclear non-compliance - Published The UN nuclear watchdog has referred Iran to the Security Council for "non-compliance" with its obligations under the non-proliferation treaty - the first such move in 20 years. The board of governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) passed a resolution at a meeting in Vienna. It cites a lack of information on Iran's nuclear material such as its stockpile of highly enriched uranium, and the lack of access to nuclear facilities for IAEA inspectors. Tehran condemned the IAEA decision, blaming US and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting inspections. New sanctions are nonetheless unlikely because Iran's allies China and Russia have veto powers in the council. The IAEA resolution - tabled by the UK, France, Germany and the US - was backed by 23 countries, with eight abstentions. China, Russia and Niger voted against. The document , externalasks IAEA chief Rafael Grossi to report Iran to the Security Council. Iran had repeatedly warned the IAEA against passing such a resolution. "They attack Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal process of verification, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to issue a resolution," Iranian deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi wrote in a post on X. The IAEA has not had access to Iran's nuclear facilities since Israel and the US carried out a number of strikes on those sites during a 12-day conflict in June 2025. The sites were targeted again in the latest war, launched by Israel and the US on 28 February. Iran says the attacks on its facilities, including uranium enrichment plants in Natanz and Fordo, are the reason it does not let IAEA inspectors visit these sites. Tehran also wants such access to be part of a wider settlement with the US and Israel to end the war. Iran has repeatedly stated that its nuclear programme is solely for peaceful purposes. The US, Israel and a number of European countries have questioned this claim, amid concerns that Tehran is trying to build a nuclear weapon. At the start of the latest US-Israel war against Iran, Tehran had roughly 440kg (970lb) of 60% enriched uranium, according to senior US officials. The material can be fairly quickly enriched to the 90% threshold needed for weapons-grade uranium. - Published3 days ago

item.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98679wr78do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win - Published German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers. Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved. Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up. Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions. It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany. The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations". The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants. Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set. Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin". While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency. Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch." Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function. As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy. Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany. "You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one. The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier. Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right. - Published2 days ago

item.title: US to ban imports of some Canadian alcohol, dairy goods and motorbikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99dm1000p7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US to ban imports of some Canadian alcohol, dairy goods and motorbikes - Published The US will ban imports of a range of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, some dairy goods and motorbikes, after its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on American goods came into force. In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said Canada was "discriminating" against the US and outlined the bans, which will begin on 29 September. Officials on both sides have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's trade minister, said the latest US measures were "unjustified" and that he would work to protect the country's workers, families and businesses. "Our core focus is on what we can control: building strength at home, diversifying our partnerships abroad, and building Canada strong for all Canadians," LeBlanc said. He said he had contacted his US counterpart and promised to work "in good faith" to resolve tensions. Earlier on Tuesday, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's move away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost". The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The two countries have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other. Generally more than two-thirds of Canada's total exports go to the US. In 2025, Canada's exports of alcoholic spirits to the US were worth US$687m (£507m), dairy products were worth $269m and motorbikes were worth $90m, according to UN data compiled by Trading Economics. But Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said the import ban covered just 0.25% of Canada's exports to the US. He said: "Nonetheless, Trump's willingness to impose an import ban is further evidence, if it were needed, that these latest measures are about inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue." - What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans - Published13 hours ago - The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts - Published31 August Canada is the second-largest trading partner of the US after Mexico. Its exports are less diversified than those of the US. In recent months, business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall. Last month, the White House imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down. Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as some sporting and fishing equipment businesses. Canada responded with what Carney called "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday. Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting American goods while not doing the same to the same products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday. Some products, like whey and non-alcoholic beer, have been banned from import entirely, while tariffs have been further hiked for others, including for cheeses and cheese substitutes - which were not covered by bans - and for motorboats. The list of Canadian products banned by the White House include: - Some dairy products like whey - Cane molasses - Non-alcoholic beer - A long list of wine, rum and vodka products - Beer made from malt - Motorbikes, including mopeds Those facing higher import taxes include: - Various types of cheese - Raw hides and skins - Paper - Some furniture and mattresses - Some metals, including aluminium and iron - Motorboats - Golf carts - Fishing rod parts and accessories - Switchboards Washington has targeted "significant industries" for Canada, including its politically influential dairy businesses, said economics lecturer Scott French from the University of New South Wales in Australia. Trump has previously argued that Canada's system - which has production quotas, set pricing, and import limits on dairy, eggs, and poultry - is unreasonable to US farmers. - Canada's 'powerful' dairy sector is in Trump's trade crosshairs - Published23 July The import bans and new tariffs will also put Canada's leaders under more pressure to resist Trump's demands for concessions, French said. The trade war will be "costly for both sides due to the historical level of integration of the North American economy," he said, adding that consumers on both sides will end up as "the biggest losers". On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moved manufacturing there. Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging levies have upset many of the States' traditional allies. Some Canadians have led a massive boycott of US products like alcohol, which have vanished from some store shelves after Trump launched his global tariff campaign last year. Trade expert Deborah Elms, from the Hinrich Foundation, told the BBC the import ban could have a "strong" impact on any Canadian business with US buyers, though early estimates show a "modest impact" affecting around $1bn worth of goods. Canada will likely "hold course for now" and adjust their business support measures to account for the US' latest moves, Elms said. "The bigger question is what it will take for the two sides to sit back down together. The language in these proclamations, as an example, isn't helpful in getting to the negotiating table," she added. Carney said on Tuesday as Canada's counter-tariffs came into effect: "There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still." Tension between the US and Canada has also moved beyond tariffs. In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some in the US. item.title: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94jgy7e94o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway - Published Dozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last respects to King Harald V in Oslo. Thousands of people lined the route during a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon, nearly two weeks after the king died aged 89. After the ceremony and burial, the Norwegian royal family, including the new King Haakon, his wife Queen Mette-Marit, and his mother and Harald's widow Queen Sonja greeted crowds from the palace balcony. A minute's silence was also observed throughout the country. Harald, who was seen as a popular, modernising figure, was on the Norwegian throne for 35 years. After 13 days of national mourning, the day began on Wednesday with ceremonial troops assembling at Akershus Fortress, the medieval castle where Harald was later laid to rest. A procession then took place, with Haakon, his sister Princess Märtha Louise and his children Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, following the late king's coffin on foot. Mette-Marit, who recently underwent a successful lung transplant, and Sonja, 89, followed in a car. Prince William, representing his father King Charles III, attended the funeral alongside the Princess Royal, who was there in a personal capacity as godmother to Norway's new monarch. They were among 30 royal figures from Sweden, Jordan, Monaco, Belgium, Spain, Japan and Denmark. Among the non-royal heads of state attending the funeral were Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier along with five foreign prime ministers. During the funeral service at the cathedral, Mette-Marit was seen wiping her eyes, as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre delivered a eulogy, saying Harald had struck "a balance between being stately and down-to-earth and that he had "made Norway greater". Queen Sonja, who was also visibly emotional during the ceremony, laid a red rose on Harald's coffin. A poignant moment as three bell tolls marking the end of a minute's silence in the cathedral was briefly interrupted by a mobile phone alarm going off. The day after his death, his son Haakon VIII thanked him for "being such a good dad" and said he had "always stayed true" to his values and commitments. Royal observers have described the late king as well respected and beloved, and who was seen as a "grandfather" of the nation. In the final months of his life, he and his family had faced personal challenges and scandal. Earlier this year, documents revealed Mette-Marit's frequent contact with Jeffrey Epstein. She later said she wished she had never met the late sex offender. Meanwhile, her son, Marius Borg Høiby - who is not a royal figure himself but grew up within the family - was given a four-year jail term for two counts of rape in June. Høiby, who is under house arrest pending appeal, was granted permission to attend the funeral, and sat in the second row during the cathedral ceremony alongside Märtha Louise's children. At the end of the service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a "missing man" formation. Harald's casket was then carried in a procession to the Palace Chapel at Akershus Fortress, where a private ceremony was attended by family members, foreign royals and other guests including the country's prime minister. King Harald was laid to rest there alongside several members of the royal family, including his father King Olav V, his mother Crown Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud. Norwegian flags across Oslo were raised from half mast to the top to mark the end of the burial, while the royal family returned to the royal palace. In a display of gratitude for the support they had received since the king's death on 28 August, the family - Haakon, Mette-Marit, Ingrid Alexandra, Sverre Magnus and Sonja - then appeared on the balcony to greet tens of thousands of people who had gathered outside.

item.title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games, says military chief
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3d7pzyjzllo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games, says military chief - Published Uganda is pulling out of the Invictus Games, a sports event for wounded military veterans run by the Duke of Sussex, only two months after the country said it would join. General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of defence and son of the president, made the announcement in a social media post on X. He said the decision to withdraw from the games was "in order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III". Ugandan government spokesman Alan Kasujja confirmed this to the BBC: "General Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People's Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know." - King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals - Published2 days ago - Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move - Published26 August The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals. A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision. "In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post. "We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval." However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel. A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda. Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived." There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission. The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women. item.title: Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and two other aides, public records show
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c046rxw93xlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and two other aides, public records show - Published President Donald Trump gave sizable cash gifts to four White House staffers, including $45,000 (£33,000) to his close aide Natalie Harp, financial disclosures released by his administration show. Two staff members got the same amount as Harp, while his longtime aide and director of Oval Office Operations, Walt Nauta, received $22,000. No other White House staffer has declared any gifts from the president, the documents show. Federal employees are prohibited from receiving outside compensation for their duties. The White House has described the gifts as personal in nature, unrelated to the staffers' work and legal under US law. In a statement provided to the BBC, a White House official said that the president "has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector". "The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals' official government duties, and are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards," the official added. The cash gifts, totalling $157,000, are marked as a "cash gift for the holidays" for Nauta, Harp and two other officials: communications advisor Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, a White House aide who serves as Trump's executive assistant. The White House did not answer a separate query from the BBC on why the other 91 listed staff members - including other top aides and First Lady Melania Trump's top advisors - did not receive gifts. The four recipients of the cash gifts are among those widely considered as close to the US president. Harp, 35, is among Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides. She is often trusted with typing out his frequent Truth Social posts, among other responsibilities. Last month, she was thrust into the national spotlight after she was named as one of a small number of people who stayed with Trump as he secretly swapped planes leaving Turkey last month. Nauta, a US Navy veteran, has also long been at Trump's side. He served as a White House military valet to the president in his first term, and later joined him as an assistant at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida after he left office. In June 2023, he was indicted alongside Trump on charges that he mishandled national security documents. The case was ultimately dismissed. The third recipient, Margo Martin, is well known for documenting Trump's activities on social media. While the final recipient, 26-year-old Chamberlain Harris, officially serves as the president's executive assistant. In February, she was also appointed to the US Commission of Fine Arts which oversees the construction of the White House ballroom and other Trump-directed projects in Washington. Cassandra Burke Roberston, a law professor and director of the Center for Professional Ethics at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that "it's not an easy call" to say whether the cash gifts were ethical or not. "If it were compensation, it's not allowed," she said. "Of course, that's where the administration's argument comes in, that it's a social gift done out of friendship. Not compensation." Additionally, Robertson said that even if legal, the gifts - along with recent controversies involving prediction markets and cryptocurrencies - could raise eyebrows among the public. "It does add to a generalised perception of really rampant conflicts of interest," she said. There are no other known instances of a serving US president giving cash gifts to staffers at the White House. Many presidents, however, have given souvenirs or personal mementos to staff. President Barack Obama, for example, gave former press secretary Robert Gibbs a framed necktie that he had once borrowed ahead of the Democratic National Convention in 2004. item.title: N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0zqk2w92lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog - Published North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern". The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium. In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said Pyongyang had also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site. These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments. "The continuation and further development of the DPRK's [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week. The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year. In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility. Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report. Despite running one of the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m. "What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC. "Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites." The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said. It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon. The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017. The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017. In August, South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, proposed talks with North Korea on officially ending the war between the two countries, adding that this could serve as a forum for discussing "effective ways to halt the advancement of the North's nuclear capabilities". North Korea has yet to respond to the proposal. North Korea declared itself a nuclear power in 2022 and vowed never to relinquish its weapons, of which it is estimated to possess dozens. Lee previously said Pyongyang was producing 15 to 20 more warheads annually, telling the BBC last year he would back a deal between US President Donald Trump and Kim to freeze production. item.title: Two die at Moldovan border as Russia-Ukraine drone war rages
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgyvpxe3yjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two die at Moldovan border as Russia-Ukraine drone war rages - Published Two people died when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The Starokozache crossing was shut after the overnight attack. Images from the scene show several burnt-out cars amid the debris. In Kyiv, a woman was killed and 14 people, including two children, were injured after a Russian drone hit a nine-storey building, officials said, while in Sumy three people died after a drone struck a shopping centre. In Russia, officials said four people, including a child, were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, while a drone hit an industrial facility in the Arctic city of Novy Urengoy. In the north-eastern city of Sumy, 20 people were also injured in the attack on the shopping mall on Wednesday evening, regional head Oleg Hryhorov said. He said efforts to deal with the aftermath were ongoing. Russia and Ukraine recently stepped up long-range strikes, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war. Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the attack at the Starokozache road crossing, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further". The crossing, about 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional head Oleh Kiper said. A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry. Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year. "Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media. "Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility." Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russia's defence ministry said its forces had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones overnight. Novorossiysk – in the south of the country - was hit hardest in what governor Veniamin Kondratiev described as a "massive overnight enemy drone attack". As well as the four deaths, 29 people were injured, and damage was reported to residential buildings, a church and a preschool. In Novy Urengoy, a drone attack on an "industrial facility" was repelled, regional governor Dmitry Artyukhov said. He added that the falling drone wreckage had triggered a fire but no-one had been injured. Ukraine's military said late on Wednesday that it had hit the Novourengoysky ZPKT - a major oil refinery located more than 3,000km from Ukraine's border. It said the facility's petroleum products and gas condensate were being used by Russia to continue its war effort. The strikes come a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke to US President Donald Trump by phone about efforts to end the war. The Trump administration has been pressing for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv saying they could take place this month. The Kremlin, however, has said it is too early to discuss a date or venue. The call followed Saturday's talks between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Putin in Moscow, before the pair travelled to Kyiv for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday. - Published1 day ago

item.title: Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62mn90ppnro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial - Published The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter. D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder. In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses. The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer. Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter. In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old. Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times. "At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday. They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life". In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard. Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security. Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported. In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty. In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution. "If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney. Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year. Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit. - Published31 August - Published28 July

item.title: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlwekrl3dqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules - Published Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public. De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves". The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation. De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place. While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word." The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities. But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro. Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation. De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent. According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun. They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date. Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals. Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security. De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year. Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang. Related topics - Published27 August

item.title: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgwydke178o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree - Published The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from officials more than a month later. Her demands have been echoed by a community in the southern US state that has been left shocked and angry. After weeks of silence, police on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that they were investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, 29, as a potential homicide - while clarifying that her official cause of death has yet to be confirmed. Authorities discovered Fortune's body on 3 August, hanging from a tree in the lot of an abandoned home. Local concern over her death has been heightened by the fact that the state has a dark history of racial violence and lynchings. The majority-black city has been left on edge. As the question lingers as to how Fortune died, petitions online signed by tens of thousands of people have called for more transparency, and members of US Congress have asked for federal intervention. "It's making me angry," Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said. "What is the hold up?" Spivey described desperate attempts to understand the status of the investigation and how multiple enquiries to police had gone unanswered. The first update she had received from authorities in weeks came in a public city meeting on Tuesday evening as Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney discussed the case and said the department "has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide". Brackney, in a statement to the BBC, elaborated and said the department always treats any pending death case as a "potential homicide" so that crucial evidence is not lost as police wait on autopsy results. The department, though, had only previously described the case as a death investigation. Tuesday's statement from Brackney said "we are conducting the investigation at the highest appropriate level while we await the medical examiner's findings", which would include an official cause and manner of death. The medical examiner's office said it would not comment on the pending case. Spivey last saw her daughter alive on 26 July, when Fortune had travelled from Mississippi, where she had lived for roughly the last decade, to Kentucky, where Spivey lives, for a family reunion. The next time she saw her daughter - in a funeral home, days before her burial - she could barely look at her body. "I didn't look straight at her. Her daddy did," she said. "I kind of looked from the side." Spivey remembered their last conversation. "She was talking about, you know, maybe even coming home," she explained. Fortune's death has left the community concerned that racial violence in Mississippi could be on the rise again. And in the absence of concrete details about the case, their suspicions are left to fester. Fortune's death was the third incident in Mississippi in less than a year where police found someone dead and hanged from a tree. The other two bodies - one black male, one white - were discovered in September 2025, on the exact same day. Both were ruled a suicide, though the mother of one of the deceased - Trey Reed - contests those findings. Fed-up residents have launched an online petition, which has gathered more than 50,000 signatures, for an independent investigation into the state's chief medical examiner, Dr Staci Turner, over the handling of a recent spate of cases involving people of colour. Another petition asks for the FBI to launch an investigation into Fortune's death The BBC has asked Turner for comment. Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes has also expressed concerns about the police investigation, saying he'd been outside the home where Fortune was thought to have lived multiple times and has never seen officers. "All cases are important, but this one - a hanging in Mississippi - should rise to the top of the food chain," Stokes said. He told the BBC he sent letters to both federal prosecutors at the Mississippi US attorney's office and the FBI weeks ago, urging that the investigation was "in dire need of assistance". He has yet to hear back from either. "Nothing from nobody," Stokes said. "It's like nobody cares." The BBC has reached out to the Mississippi US attorney's office and the local FBI office for comment. US Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett has similarly requested federal intervention. In a letter to the US Department of Justice, she asked for an investigation into recent deaths in Mississippi - including that of Tasia Fortune - calling them "possible cases of modern-day lynchings". She cited the state's "appalling historical reputation of violent terrorism against black Americans". In addition to Mississippi, there have been multiple other cases nationally of black Americans found hanged from trees, including four in North Carolina this year alone. Three were ruled a suicide. An autopsy is pending for the fourth death. The BBC has reached out to the justice department for comment. Stokes is clear that he does not know whether Fortune's death was a lynching, or whether race played a part at all. Nor does he care. He just wants answers. Brandon King, president of the student National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chapter at nearby Jackson State University, said the mystery of Fortune's death, combined with minimal updates from police, has led him and others to be "extra cautious" around campus. The feeling, King said, was that "hey, you could be next. This is in Jackson. This is in your backyard". The thought is extra worrying, he continued, because "this is supposed to be the capital. This is where I'm supposed to feel the most safe". As for Spivey, she cried before heading to a funeral home for her daughter, dreading having to fill out a death certificate and decide whether to cremate or bury her firstborn child. She wanted to cremate her daughter but decided, in the end, for a burial. She said she was holding out hope there would be updates in the investigation, which might mean needing to exhume her corpse.

========================================
White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern - Published The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness. The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website. On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously". The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown. "At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game. "To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community." The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder. Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website. "Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall. Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake. When players run into the edge of the map, a "Deported" number shows how many people the player was able to catch. The games have drawn criticism from politicians, with Connecticut Democratic state senator Matt Lesser tweeting, external: "Heating oil is near an all-time high but hey you can play Border Tsar Tom Homan in a video game". Video games and The White House The arcade section is just one example of how the Trump administration has increasingly incorporated video game culture into its political messaging on social media. In October 2025, the official White House X account drew criticism for posting an AI-generated picture of President Trump, external in a suit from the video game Halo. Meanwhile on 6 March it posted a video which mixed footage of US military strikes in Iran with film and TV clips, as well a clip from Halo's protagonist Master Chief saying "finishing this fight". The post was condemned by the Master Chief voice actor Steve Downes in a now-deleted tweet which called for "the producers of this disgusting and juvenile war porn" to remove his voice from the video. The Pokémon Company International also criticised the White House's use of its imagery in March, when it included a tiny version of the popular character Pikachu in a meme posted online with the phrase "Make America Great Again". item.title: Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgynv90599o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry - Published Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there. Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong. Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia. Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway. The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials. They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored. Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road. "The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said. "The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway." The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry. Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days. A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said. Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old. Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said. Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years. The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha. There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN. Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting. International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws. Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors. This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India. In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

item.title: Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement
item.description:

========================================
Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement - Published A South Korean court has ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay his ex-wife 2.55tr won ($1.87bn; £1.38bn) in assets, marking the largest divorce settlement in the country's history. Kwon, who founded South Korea's third-largest video game company Smilegate, is one of the country's richest men. Bloomberg puts his net worth at $3bn. Smilegate was wholly owned by him until Wednesday when a court ruled that a 35% stake, valued at about 2.5tr won, be transferred to his wife Lee Hwa-jin. He was also ordered to pay her an additional 65bn won in cash. This settlement is more than double the previous record of 944bn won which tech titan Chey Tae-won was ordered to pay his ex-wife. In filing for divorce with Kwon, Lee had sought a 50% stake in Smilegate. Her lawyers argued that she had helped finance the company at its founding, according to Bloomberg. Kwon and Lee got married in 2001, a year before he founded Smilegate. Its best-known titles include the first-person shooter game CrossFire and the action role-playing game Lost Ark. Lee also said she spent more than 20 years raising their children and caring for their household. Kwon in turn argued that Lee neither invested nor worked for the company. Earlier this year, Smilegate published a statement saying all of the company's initial capital came from Kwon. A Smilegate spokesperson declined to "comment on the major shareholder's personal matters". "We will continue to faithfully perform our duties as usual," they said in a statement cited by The Chosun Daily. Both parties can still challenge the ruling. In July this year, Chey Tae-won, the chairman of the corporate giant SK Group, was ordered to pay his ex-wife 944bn won which, prior to today's ruling, was the largest divorce award in Korean history. However, this was later struck down by the Supreme Court who cited a miscalculation that increased the value of the couple's assets. It has ordered the case to be reviewed.

item.title: 'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmr22kpd9yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests - Published The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa. His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours. "When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal. The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand. Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts. Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go". Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged. The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term. In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs. "Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said. The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency". "I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October. He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month. A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given. "For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added. The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week. Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages. He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network. "We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience." Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.
