item.title: Hong Kong's first leader after British handover dies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn457lq938jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hong Kong's first leader after British handover dies - Published Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89. The former shipping scion took over the reins from the last British Governor Chris Patten in July 1997 when the UK handed Hong Kong back to China, ending more than 150 years of British control. Tung's rocky tenure was marked by the Asian Financial Crisis, two major epidemics, and historic protests which attracted criticism of his administration. He eventually resigned in 2005. Tung died on Tuesday night surrounded by loved ones, local media reported. His office described him as a man "devoted to his country and its people". Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from Liverpool University in the UK before moving to the US, where he worked at General Electric for almost a decade. In 1969, he moved to Hong Kong and worked in his father's shipping conglomerate, the Orient Overseas, eventually taking over the reins in 1979. His political career began in 1992 when he was appointed a member of Patten's executive council. Despite having little political experience, Tung was believed to be handpicked by Beijing to lead Hong Kong after the handover. He was seen as a loyalist, especially after China's state-run banks helped rescue his family business during a global slump in the mid-1980s. During a reception at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996, China's then-president Jiang Zemin walked across a packed room to shake Tung's hands – a widely photographed gesture that at the time famously signalled Beijing's backing of Tung for the top job. The Asian Financial Crisis hit shortly after Tung took over, which sent home prices diving. His administration was also beset by a series of public health challenges, including a bird flu outbreak from 1997 to 2002 and the 2003 outbreak of Sars, also known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome. But Tung's biggest political challenge took place in July 2003 during his second term, when half a million Hongkongers took to the streets to protest against a proposed national security law they feared would threaten their civic rights. His administration abandoned the proposed legislation following the massive outcry, which also contributed to Tung stepping down in March 2005. At the time his declining health was cited as a reason - but some said he was pressured by Beijing to step down. Beijing ultimately imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which authorities have argued is necessary to maintain stability. Critics however have called it "the end of Hong Kong" and say it has created a climate of fear in the city. Tung's last public outing was in July 2021, at an event marking the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. He underwent heart surgery months later, according to reports. He is survived by his wife and three children. Hong Kong's former chief executives have paid tribute to Tung. Leung Chun-ying, who led the city between 2012 and 2017, described him as a "benevolent" leader who "won people over with reason". Carrie Lam, who was the chief executive from 2017 to 2022, said Tung's leadership made "a historic contribution with lasting benefits". China's state news agency Xinhua called Tung a "renowned patriot, distinguished social activist, close friend of the Communist Party of China". It also noted that Tung had served as one of many vice-chairmen of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body, for four consecutive terms.

item.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv2vwjjq3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report - Published Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found. The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year. When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement." The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings. About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials. After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter. The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children. When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations. The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children. But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough. Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material "Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu. The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC. According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act. TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad. According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps. "Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said. TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live. For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards." For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad. When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000". TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed. This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down. Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings. TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers. The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM. Meta has said it prohibits, external promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images. One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them". "We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added. The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80]. Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform. Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to. After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems". But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China. These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions. TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

item.title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8jd14glvneo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands - Published The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands. The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean. Reacting to the news, Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill insisted that there could be "no doubt" about the British government's commitment to the Falkland Islanders. Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, McNeill said that "the decision by the Falkland Islands government to pursue hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for them to take alongside the commercial companies involved". She added that "the future of the Falkland Islands is for Falkland Islanders to determine". The simmering dispute between Britain and Argentina over the Falklands heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands. Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas. In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that." The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty. He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory. Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination". The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering". Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives. Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028. The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities. "The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted. Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development". Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. Related topics - Published4 days ago

item.title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyrjw1yj75o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on - Published The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history". But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out. Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back. The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family. On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center. "After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind. - New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links - Published2 days ago Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious". A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted. Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants. The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges. Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028. But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial. "My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said. "Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added. Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims. Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about. "I want to concentrate on the memories," he said. "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'." Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died. "They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones." Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda. He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z". But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse". He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial. Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case. "Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University. She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions. John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case. The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well." During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office. Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice. "If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts." Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial. The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm. Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing. - In court with the '9/11 mastermind', two decades after his arrest - Published10 January 2025 - The '9/11 mastermind' wants to plead guilty. Why is the US trying to stop him? - Published10 January 2025 Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency. Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions. "My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are. I just want them convicted," he said. Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal. "It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said. Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there. "My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial." With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event". "I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended." When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year. Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in". "If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained. As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo. "It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

item.title: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ydlex9yn3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades - Published Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is. Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage. Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction. The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves. They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada. Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful. For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there. Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that. Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected. And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking. As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors. That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable. Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades. Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage. Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment. But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal. Most would disagree vehemently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah. But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive. For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress. The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise". In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship". Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed. The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank. Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it. In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories. But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans. Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God. So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

item.title: Hegseth is shaking up the Pentagon as the US wages war - but at what cost?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94j8e9n12o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hegseth is shaking up the Pentagon as the US wages war - but at what cost? - Published The United States military is at the centre of a fight on two fronts. First is President Donald Trump's attempt to prise the Strait of Hormuz from Iran's grip; the latest phase of his stalemated war in the Gulf which is drawing in US forces and equipment from around the globe. The second is a culture war at home in which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is conducting a promised shake-up at the Pentagon, sparking bitter recriminations and a string of departures including the top civilian in charge of the US Army last week. The upheaval has triggered questions that could shape the legacy of Trump's second term. Is the US military being stretched to a point that could risk global security? And are these shifts leaving America's extraordinary global network of alliances vulnerable? Last Monday there was dramatic news from the Pentagon. One of its most senior political leaders, Dan Driscoll, stepped down as US Secretary of the Army. Driscoll is not exactly a household name in America, let alone outside it. But his departure mattered. It was the latest twist in a power struggle within the fortress-like walls of the Pentagon over the future of the world's most formidable fighting force. Driscoll had clashed repeatedly with Hegseth over the nature and speed of military reform. His departure was the latest in a long line of top leaders removed or sidelined by Hegseth. The level of concern became clear as one Republican Senator Thom Tillis - a frequent Trump critic - called for Hegseth to be fired. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," he said. "This is not good news. You know, for our nation, for the army," H.R. McMaster, who served as Trump's National Security Adviser during his first term, told CBS when asked about Driscoll's departure. "Secretary Driscoll was pushing… a modernisation agenda to catch the army up." The backstory of Driscoll's resignation cut deep into issues about the readiness of the US Army. Driscoll wanted urgent modernisation by adding drones throughout ordinary army formations to make it adept for 21st Century warfare. He said the Ukraine war had shown how the battlefield had changed, with cheap drones and anti-missile systems challenging the US military with its vast bureaucracy and expensive procurement processes. Hegseth had in fact initiated much of this modernisation plan but subsequently came into conflict with Driscoll, according to reports, as well as with others advocating its rapid expansion. A source familiar with last week's departure told the BBC's US partner CBS News that Driscoll had raised concerns within the administration about army readiness and transformation, which Driscoll said Hegseth was "blocking" specifically by firing the generals responsible. Jon Duffy, a retired Navy captain and former White House defence policy official, said Driscoll's resignation showed how far Hegseth had "hollowed out" the military leadership at a critical moment. "You lose the [army] secretary, the chief of staff and other senior leaders driving modernisation, it creates a lot of uncertainty and it disrupts momentum," he said. "That uncertainty at leadership levels has downstream effects on the force," added Duffy, who had a 30-year career and commanded US warships before joining the White House during the second Obama administration. In public, Hegseth - a former Army National Guardsman and Fox News pundit - has spent much of his time calling for cultural change to the US military. He has vowed to end what he called "woke" initiatives and scrap "stupid" rules of engagement he said constrained war fighters' "lethality". He tore up diversity programmes, banned beards and railed against seeing "fat generals in the halls of the Pentagon". He removed or sidelined the top uniformed officers in charge of the Army, Navy and Air Force as well as at least two dozen generals, admirals and civilian defence leaders, including some of the US military's most decorated officers, often with little explanation. One critic compares the changes in the top ranks to President Xi Jinping's political purges of the Chinese military which are said to have left serious deficiencies in command structure and readiness. "We've been conducting a military purge as well, and that has real effects on the ability of our military to be able to discharge its responsibilities," Michael Schiffer, a former top Pentagon official who covered East Asia from 2009 to 2012 under the Obama presidency, told the BBC. "The way in which [Hegseth is] shaking them up… is bringing on board an awful lot of risk without any apparent way to be able to address or ameliorate it," said Schiffer, who is now a senior fellow at the liberal think-tank the Center for American Progress. Asked last week about Driscoll's departure, Vice-President JD Vance defended Hegseth, saying he was in "strident agreement" about the need for a culture shift after what he called 40 years of lost wars and "military misadventures". "What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America," Vance said. - US army secretary resigns after months of tension - Published1 September - US Navy chief leaving post 'effective immediately', Pentagon says - Published23 April - What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow - Published27 August In a statement, the White House told the BBC that President Trump had "full confidence in Secretary Hegseth and the entire Department of War whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself". Trump has continued to back Hegseth, standing by him during controversies such as Signalgate and describing him in a phone interview with NBC News last month as "actually one of my best". Ezra Cohen, a former Under Secretary of Defence during the first Trump administration, described Hegseth's reforms as "bringing in fresh thinking and a more forward-leaning attitude". But the reported friction among the military leadership and the stalemate with Iran has raised questions about the future of the US military at a critical moment. 'Vulnerabilities in Europe' Trump's order to launch strikes on Iran on 28 February led to a significant global redistribution of US military resources over the subsequent months. US weapons stored in Europe and Asia were transferred from those regions to replenish supplies in the Gulf. Europe is now feeling significant "blowback", according to Professor Liana Fix, a Germany-based expert at the Council on Foreign Relations. She said the lack of communication by the Trump administration with its Nato and European allies ahead of the attack on Iran left relations reeling and accelerated a strategic decision already in process to shift some US military resources away from Europe, particularly as Trump complained that his European allies weren't helping. Prof Fix said in that context Russian President Vladimir Putin had escalated so-called "hybrid" attacks involving armed drones or sabotage attacks on Nato countries like Germany. Russia denies carrying out the attacks. "What [Putin] is seeing is not a united stance from the United States and the Europeans to further increase pressure on Russia… he sees that they are weakening, that there are windows and openings of vulnerabilities in Europe," she told the BBC. Last month, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid a highly unusual visit to Moscow. He is reported to have delivered a warning to the Kremlin not to test Nato's resolve. But at the same time, one of Hegseth's top officials at the Pentagon, Elbridge Colby, was in Europe to push countries to spend more on their own defence. Washington had announced a cut of 5,000 from a total 40,000 US troops based in Germany, while a Biden-era plan to deploy a US battalion with long-range Tomahawk missiles to the country was being dropped. The drawdowns in Europe fit the Trump administration's strategy that predates the Iran war. It sees the Pacific region and Washington's rivalry with China as America's number one national security challenge. But while the fallout from the Iran war has exacerbated Trump's irritation with Europe and accelerated some US military moves away from the region, it has not been to the immediate benefit of the US presence in the Pacific. In fact, Washington has also pulled resources from there. Carrier forces were diverted from the Pacific to the Gulf, including the USS Abraham Lincoln and later the Japan-based USS George Washington. The war is widely assessed to have left critical stocks of American ammunition badly depleted. The US fired about a third of its 3,000-strong stockpile of Tomahawk attack missiles, according to the Washington DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). Its air defence munitions were burned up at an even higher rate, with nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors - used to shoot down aircraft and cruise and ballistic missiles - fired out of a stockpile of around 2,300, according to the CSIS. White House Principle Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said America's "military might" was "stronger than it's ever been". "The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond," she said. Meanwhile Ezra Cohen, the former Trump defence official who is now a fellow at the Hudson Institute, described the president as having degraded Iran's conventional military threat. Iran's proxy groups are weaker than ever, he said, and in many places they have been completely obliterated, meaning "the president now has additional options and forces in the region to strike other Iranian targets, including nuclear targets, at will". The strikes might yet take place again. Thousands of troops, including the 82nd Airborne Division, were sent to the Middle East more than six months ago for a deployment that is now stretching into 2027 with no obvious end in sight. Pictures last week of the USS Abraham Lincoln docking in Thailand with a rusting hull after a gruelling nine months at sea in the Gulf were pounced on by Iran. The regime tried to portray it as a symbol of America's spent efforts. Hegseth, meanwhile, forcefully rejected claims of abysmal conditions on board. But the narrative war reflected the challenge for Trump and Hegseth as they fight to transform the Pentagon while waging a costly, protracted war. With additional reporting by Cai Pigliucci

item.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx3v11de7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why? - Published The images are hard to ignore. Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation. One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra. They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state. At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner. Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation. His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products. "These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC. The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant. Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity. But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him. An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it. "I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC. Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives. In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions. "When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language. But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet. The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is. Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled. And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive. By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000. Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said. "Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible". Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public. The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram. However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic. Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed". Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons. "While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association. Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first. His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach. In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law. The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard". The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses? Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations. For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone. "Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC. He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety. "We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption." The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work. Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes. Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools. But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post. "The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal. The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds. For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets. Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban. "We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

item.title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
item.description:

========================================
AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant - Published The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes. Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future. Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres. However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future. Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history. Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. "Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI. Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it. He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples. "It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients." Job losses 'overstated' In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade. "With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do." Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI. Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said. This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March. Big Boss Interview: Arm Holdings Rene Haas The CEO of chip design company Arm tells the BBC AI will help cure cancer, lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but says its rapid growth is being held up by a shortage of chips needed in data centres. There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space." But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here. "I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those." As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London. But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge". - Published2 days ago - Published27 August - Published28 January

Land in limbo: BBC visits West Bank village in area earmarked by Israel for settlement UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have triggered a series of Israeli counter-measures against UK nationals and organisations. Watch: Norway bids farewell to King Harald Tributes have been paid to King Harald V after his funeral in Norway's capital Oslo, with the Prince of Wales and other European royals among attendees. Flags were raised from half-mast to mark the conclusion of a private ceremony at Akershus Fortress, where the king was laid to rest in the crypt of the Palace Chapel after a public service at Oslo Cathedral. Tens of thousands of people lined the streets to pay their respects after 13 days of national mourning. The new king Haakon VIII - Harald's son - and his family stood on the balcony of the Royal Palace and waved to thousands of people gathered outside. The late monarch died in August after 35 years on the throne. Where is Israel's proposed West Bank settlement the UK opposes? The BBC's Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports from Ma'ale Adumim - an existing Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, overlooking Israel's proposed E1 site. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, speaking to Parliament on Tuesday, announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank "to deter settlement expansion" and "prevent the development of E1". Israel has opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes at the proposed site. Miliband said he would ban the import of goods from Israel's "illegal settlements" in the West Bank. He also said "ethnic cleansing" was being carried out by "settler terrorists" and accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye". Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded to the move by saying that Israel will close the British consulate in Jerusalem and called the UK government "hostile". Watch: Pupils return to West Bank school behind barbed wire to protect against settlers A school in the occupied West Bank has been surrounded by barbed-wire fencing as Palestinian parents fear for their children's safety due to the rise of Israeli settler attacks in the area. The isolated village of al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, has been increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance. Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April. All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.
